extracted.intended_audience: educated political readers, statesmen, and critics of the French Revolution (late 18th-century British public)
extracted.subtask_description: A rhetorical and philosophical critique assessing the legitimacy, methods, and institutional designs of the revolutionary French government, arguing standards for prudent reform and representative constitution-making.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legitimacy requires law, necessity, or prescription
rubrics_metrics.description: A government that 'has derived its birth from no law and no necessity' lacks legitimacy; prescription (long usage) mellows into legality and is important for recognition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assemblies newly formed by revolution need a justification ('an apology') because making a revolution 'is to subvert the ancient state' — without law/necessity/prescription strangers and concerned persons will hesitate to give countenance. Anti-pattern: declaring authority without roots in law or long usage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revolutions require explicit justification
rubrics_metrics.description: To make a revolution 'is a measure which, prima fronte, requires an apology' — radical change must be justified by clear reasons because it subverts established order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The public has license to 'examine into the mode of acquiring new power' and to criticise its use; therefore revolutionaries should provide public reasons and sound justification rather than asserting authority by force alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency between means of acquiring and using power
rubrics_metrics.description: If power was obtained by 'artifices, frauds, and violences' (the arts of ambition), using it for public good should not be left to 'untried speculations'; means used to obtain power should not contradict methods of governance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observation of discrepancy between ruthless acquisition and experimental administration reveals poor spirit; avoid using tyrannical arts to gain power and then improvising governance without experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confront difficulty rather than evade it
rubrics_metrics.description: Great statesmanship confronts and overcomes difficulties, turning them into instruments for further improvement; avoiding difficulty leads to slothful, feeble, and insecure work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid tricking short-cuts and 'little fallacious facilities' — those create arbitrary governments. Valorise steady wrestling with hard problems as a means to strengthen understanding and institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve useful elements while reforming
rubrics_metrics.description: To 'preserve and to reform' requires keeping the useful parts of old establishments and fitting additions to what is retained, using sustained attention and various powers of comparison and combination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer slow, cautious methods where 'time is amongst the assistants' — incremental steps allow observation of effects and correction. Anti-pattern: wholesale abolition and total destruction as the first step in reform.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislators should possess sensibility and deliberate temper
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'true lawgiver ought to have a heart full of sensibility' — legislators must love and respect mankind and act with fear of themselves; their movements should be deliberate despite intuitive aims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislation is social work wrought by social means; mind must conspire with mind and time is required to produce union. Anti-pattern: unfeeling confidence presented as the sole qualification for legislators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid destructive haste; prefer composition over mere simplicity
rubrics_metrics.description: Violent haste and defiance of nature deliver governments to 'every projector and adventurer' and produce defective schemes; excellence lies not in simplicity but in 'excellence in composition'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not mistake the ability to destroy for ability to construct. Haste produces schemes 'feeble, vicious, and insecure'; prefer balanced, composite solutions that reconcile competing interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fix a presiding ruling principle with prolific energy
rubrics_metrics.description: Wise legislators often 'establish some sure, solid, and ruling principle in government' (a 'plastic nature') and then leave it to operate, rather than continual radical changes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A presiding principle with enduring energy is the 'criterion of profound wisdom'; avoid constant overturning of foundations for every new project or fashion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ground institutional design in experience, not speculative theories
rubrics_metrics.description: Political plans should not be founded on abstract geometrical/arithmetical schemes devoid of political principle or local knowledge; speculative organization invites 'innumerable local inconveniencies'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: dividing a country into regular squares (Departments, Communes, Cantons) by geometrical measurement neglects local circumstances and creates practical problems. Prefer empirically informed boundaries and arrangements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation must preserve individual equality
rubrics_metrics.description: Representation systems that privilege territory or contribution at the expense of individual rights undermine the 'equality of men'; placing representation on territorial masses or contributions can subvert personal equality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The threefold basis (territory/population/contribution) is inconsistent if it treats representation as a property of districts rather than individuals; design representative institutions to maintain individual political equality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid property-based qualifications that nullify natural rights
rubrics_metrics.description: Qualifications for voting or office (e.g., local valuation of three days' labour, payment of ten days' labour, direct contribution of a mark of silver) 'order him to buy the right' and establish tyranny against those with nothing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such thresholds exclude the poorest and are 'impotent to secure independence; strong only to destroy the rights of men.' Anti-pattern: minimal-seeming qualifications that nonetheless violate the principle of natural equality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimise intermediary gradations that disconnect voters and representatives
rubrics_metrics.description: A multilayered electoral process (primary assemblies electing Communes; Communes electing Departments; Departments electing National Assembly) places many barriers between primary elector and representative, destroying connexion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intermediary stages create 'turnpikes' taxing rights and weaken direct accountability; where possible preserve clearer linkage between constituents and their representatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation by contribution (tax) is inequitable and politically dangerous
rubrics_metrics.description: Using contribution (riches) as a basis for representation introduces a principle 'totally different from the equality of men' and cannot be fairly reconciled either at the individual level or by treating districts as proxies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assigning extra representation to districts because of aggregate contribution does not protect the rich individually and may inflame provincial jealousies; if any weighting is used, its justice and practical consequences must be carefully examined.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of translating literary paradoxes into political practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Paradoxes and 'the marvellous in life' that serve to interest readers (Rousseau's marvellous) should not be adopted as serious grounds for state action; writers' paradoxes become dangerous when taken literally by legislators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: treating eloquent exaggerations or rhetorical devices as practical programs for governance — this leads to impractical or harmful policies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Large political designs require multiple minds and long-term continuity
rubrics_metrics.description: When 'the great interests of mankind are concerned through a long succession of generations', councils should admit successive generations into deliberation; one age cannot supply all wisdom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design institutions and principles that allow slow development, corrective observation across steps, and contributions from minds of different ages; avoid expecting instant perfection from a single assembly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer tested remedies to alchemy and empiricism in public policy
rubrics_metrics.description: Discouraging 'alchemists and empirics' — those who reject common remedies — public policy should rely on experience and regular methods rather than speculative cures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: disdain for regular, common methods and embracing untested 'projects' that promise grand cures. Value ordinary measures and incremental improvement.
